terms.gloss: a trial, a test; an experiment; experience
evidence: Quint. 2.5.15: minus valent praecepta quam experīmenta
Plin. NH 29.18, of doctors: discunt perīculīs nostrīs et experīmenta per mortēs agunt
terms.comment: A proof, test or trial, and so what is learnt by it, experience (Lewis & Short: once in Cicero, Tusc. 3.74, common after Augustus). The scientists kept it for an experiment (Morgan–Owens). To make one: experīmentum facere, or with Prudentius experīmentum capere, to put to the test.

terms.gloss: to make trial of, test, try out
evidence: Cic. Verr. 1.34: alicujus fideī perīculum facere (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The older idiom, with the genitive of what is tried. Perīculum is first a trial; its common sense is the risk that goes with one, danger, so the phrase needs its genitive or its context to be heard as a test.

terms.gloss: try, test, put to the proof; experience
evidence: Cic. Cael. 58: vim ejus esse expertum in servō (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The verb for “to experiment”: to try a thing out, and to learn by trying.

phrases.english: Their courage grows as they try it.

phrases.latin: fac periclum in litterīs, fac in palaestrā, in mūsicīs
phrases.english: try him out in letters, in the wrestling-school, in music

phrases.latin: coctum est, dēvorā, et experīmentum cape sit crūdum an assum suāvius
phrases.english: it’s cooked: eat it up, and find out whether raw or roast tastes better
